title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Sleep — September 2026

studies.title: Sleeping nine hours or more is linked to earlier death — sleeping six is not
studies.ns_score_reason: a 30-year follow-up is unusually long, and the null result for short sleep cuts against the dominant public health message.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 3305 adults from the Chin-Shan Community Cardiovascular Cohort in Taiwan for a median of 30.8 years, sorting them by self-reported habitual sleep into short (≤6 h), normal (7–8 h) and long (≥9 h). Long sleepers had a 17% higher risk of death from any cause after adjustment; short sleepers showed no significant excess risk for all-cause or cardiovascular death. Causal mediation analysis suggested part of the long-sleep signal ran through systolic blood pressure.
studies.why_it_matters: Most sleep messaging warns about not getting enough; this cohort, with follow-up long enough to outlast reverse-causation worries about undiagnosed illness at baseline, puts the mortality signal at the other end of the distribution.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on someone who proudly gets nine hours and thinks they're doing everything right. The hook is the asymmetry: three decades of data, and it's the long sleepers who show up in the mortality column while the six-hour crowd doesn't. Call the Institute of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine team at National Taiwan University (Kuo-Liong Chien, Jiun-Yu Wang) and ask them directly why the short-sleep association vanished here when it appears in so many shorter cohorts — and push them on the blood-pressure mediation finding.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health or data-journalism outlet on the "U-shaped curve" problem in epidemiology — why long sleep keeps appearing as a risk factor across dozens of cohorts, and whether it is a cause, a symptom of something not yet diagnosed, or an artifact of how we ask people about their nights.
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation. Sleep duration was self-reported via structured questionnaire, and appears to have been measured at baseline only. Single population (one Taiwanese community cohort); may not generalize. Cardiovascular mortality association was not statistically significant.

studies.title: How you use your phone predicts depression far better than how long you use it
studies.ns_score_reason: a prospectively registered umbrella review that directly tests the assumption behind screen-time limits; pulled down by the poor quality of the underlying reviews.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A prospectively registered umbrella review synthesized 59 meta-analyses published between July 2015 and May 2026, comparing effects for "how much screen time" against "problematic or high-intensity use" across myopia, obesity, sleep, mental health and neck pain. For depression symptoms, time spent on social networking sites showed a weak association (r = 0.11) while problematic use showed a much larger one (r = 0.29). Sleep sat in between, and for myopia and obesity, general exposure mattered but problematic-use definitions did not consistently amplify the effect.
studies.why_it_matters: Screen-time guidance is built almost entirely on hours counted, yet the outcomes people worry about most — mood, sleep — track the character of use rather than its quantity, while the outcomes nobody talks about (eyesight, weight) do track hours.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the mismatch: parents and governments are counting minutes, and the minutes are the wrong number for the thing they're actually afraid of. Open on a household screen-time dashboard that reports a figure telling you almost nothing about your teenager's mood. Worth calling Nayun Ta and colleagues at Renmin University about their Outcome-Differentiated Amplification Framework — and pressing on why sleep falls awkwardly between the two patterns. Note explicitly that this is correlational synthesis, not evidence that cutting problematic use fixes depression.
studies.wider_angle: A critical piece for an education or policy outlet on the evidence base beneath screen-time rules: 56 of the 59 meta-analyses underpinning this literature were rated "critically low" quality by AMSTAR-2. That is a story about how confident guidance gets built on shaky synthesis.
studies.caveats: Umbrella review of meta-analyses, not primary data; 56/59 reviews rated critically low quality; high heterogeneity; cross-domain comparisons partly descriptive with intervals that include the null; publication-bias-corrected contrasts available for only three domains; the proposed framework is explicitly hypothesis-generating.

studies.title: Night owls don't actually sleep worse than larks — their clocks are just shifted
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean actigraphy comparison of extreme chronotypes with a largely null result that readers will find reassuring; limited by small, young, mostly female sample.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers recruited 84 young adults (mean age 23.3) selected as extreme morning types (n=42) or extreme evening types (n=42) and had them wear wrist actigraphs continuously for a week in ordinary daily life. Across quantitative and qualitative sleep measures, and across most circadian and ultradian rhythm parameters, the two groups did not differ. What did differ was phase — every measure of timing — plus the rate at which nocturnal motor inactivity deepened across the night, which was steeper in morning types.
studies.why_it_matters: Evening chronotype is routinely treated as a quasi-pathological state linked to worse sleep; in a naturalistic week, extreme owls slept as well as extreme larks and simply did it later, supporting the idea that chronotype is about synchronization with the environment rather than sleep quality.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the night owl who has been told for years that their body clock is broken. The surprise is the absence of a difference: same sleep, same rhythm strength, different phase. Call Lorenzo Tonetti at the University of Bologna, and ask about the first-ever chronotype comparison using Locomotor Inactivity During Sleep — the one measure where larks and owls genuinely diverged, and what a steeper overnight decline actually means.
studies.wider_angle: A workplace and schools piece for a general-interest outlet: if owls sleep just as well when left alone, the damage attributed to evening chronotype may be entirely an artifact of 9am start times. Frame around the social jetlag debate and the patchy evidence on later school starts.
studies.caveats: Small N (84), highly selected extreme chronotypes, narrow age range (young adults), heavily female (64/84), single center, actigraphy rather than polysomnography, and null results in a modest sample cannot rule out small real differences.

studies.title: Poor sleep and inactivity cluster together — and that pattern tracks bipolar disorder risk
studies.ns_score_reason: very large cohort with 13.8 years of follow-up and a genuinely different analytic approach; weakened by the fact that healthy-lifestyle-lowers-risk is familiar territory.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using 242,947 UK Biobank participants free of neuropsychiatric illness at baseline, researchers abandoned the usual single composite "Life's Essential 8" score and instead used latent profile analysis to find naturally occurring clusters of health behavior. Five emerged, including a distinctive "low physical activity with poor sleep" group. Over a median 13.8 years, all four healthier profiles were associated with lower anxiety (HRs 0.65–0.78) and substantially lower bipolar disorder incidence (HRs 0.37–0.51) relative to the low-score group.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests people don't have an evenly distributed "health score" — they have patterns, and a pattern in which bad sleep and inactivity travel together is separable from one built around blood pressure and lipids, with different implications for mental health risk.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is methodological but the payoff is human: averaging eight health metrics into one number hides the fact that the sleep-and-sedentary combination is its own thing. Open on the ambiguity of a single wellness score on a smartwatch. Call Xiang Gao's group at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and ask what distinguishes the poor-sleep/low-activity profile from simply scoring badly overall — and be clear this is observational risk stratification, not a treatment claim.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist psychiatry or data outlet: the bipolar disorder result rests on just 341 incident cases and schizophrenia on 40, in a cohort of nearly a quarter of a million. A piece on why UK Biobank — the workhorse of modern epidemiology — is badly underpowered for rare psychiatric outcomes, and what that means for the flood of papers using it.
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation. Very few incident bipolar (341) and schizophrenia (40) cases; the schizophrenia finding is explicitly exploratory and null. UK Biobank participants are healthier and less diverse than the general population. Sleep health assessed as a single self-reported component.

studies.title: Ultramarathon runners get 96 minutes of sleep during a 217km race — and hallucinate
studies.ns_score_reason: vivid, objectively measured natural experiment in extreme sleep restriction; small N and male-only.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Fifteen male athletes (mean age 45.1) in the Brazil 135 Ultramarathon wore wrist actigraphs for seven days before, throughout, and seven days after the race, covering 135km or 217km routes. Mean total sleep during the race was 96.67 minutes. Nearly every runner reported symptoms of insufficient sleep — sleepiness, loss of balance, and in four cases hallucinations. Crucially, how much a runner slept during the race was uncorrelated with finish time.
studies.why_it_matters: This is one of the few datasets where objectively measured, days-long sleep restriction happens voluntarily in the field rather than in a lab, and it shows that sleeping less during the event bought no performance advantage while producing frank perceptual disturbance.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a runner seeing things that aren't there somewhere on a Brazilian highway at 3am. The surprise is the non-finding: sleeping less didn't make anyone faster, so the sleep that runners sacrifice on the assumption it's costing them time appears to buy nothing. Call Andrea Maculano Esteves at UNICAMP, who tracked these athletes for more than two weeks. Also worth noting the athletes entered the race already sleep-deprived — most were under eight hours with poor efficiency in the week before.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature on hallucination under extreme exertion and sleep loss — how common it is in ultra-endurance sport, what the reported content looks like, and what it tells us about how quickly waking perception degrades. Fits a sports or general-interest magazine, and pairs naturally with research on solo sailors and polar expeditions.
studies.caveats: Small N (15 enrolled, sleep data for 13), male only, no control group, symptoms self-reported, actigraphy is unreliable during sustained low-level movement, and several key comparisons were non-significant trends (P = .058).

studies.title: Moderate drinkers have enlarged choroid plexus — and it tracks their sleep problems
studies.ns_score_reason: a nearly 800-person imaging dataset pointing at an overlooked brain structure in people who are not alcohol-dependent; the sex-split sleep findings are messy.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using structural MRI from 796 Human Connectome Project participants aged 22–37, researchers compared 399 moderate-to-heavy drinkers with 397 light or non-drinkers. Heavy drinkers had significantly larger choroid plexus volumes on both sides, with no difference in total cerebrospinal fluid volume — arguing against simple brain atrophy. Within the heavy-drinking group, choroid plexus volume correlated with sleep latency and sleep disturbance scores on the PSQI, and with total PSQI score in men.
studies.why_it_matters: The choroid plexus is a neuro-immune gateway that barely features in popular understanding of the brain, and this identifies it as a candidate early structural marker of alcohol's effects in young people who would not be diagnosed as dependent.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the structure nobody has heard of: the brain's blood–CSF border post, bigger in people who drink a few times a week, and bigger still in those who lie awake longest. Open on the gap between "not a problem drinker" and "not unaffected." Call Alan Francis at UT Rio Grande Valley, and ask about the strangest result in the paper — heavy-drinking women reported *better* sleep efficiency and duration than light-drinking women, while heavy-drinking men reported worse. Make clear this is cross-sectional imaging, not evidence that drinking causes the enlargement.
studies.wider_angle: A neuroscience feature on the choroid plexus itself for a specialist or long-form science outlet — from CSF plumbing to its emerging role as an immune interface in aging, depression and neurodegeneration, with alcohol as the newest entry on the list.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational — cannot establish causation or direction. Sleep entirely self-reported (PSQI). Sex-stratified findings are contradictory and unexplained. Secondary analysis of an existing open dataset not designed for this question. Drinking groups defined by questionnaire.

studies.title: Camera-tracked cribs reveal how a baby's temperament locks in their sleep pattern
studies.ns_score_reason: nightly objective sleep data from 208 infants plus a within-person modeling approach most infant-sleep research can't do; commercial monitor recruitment limits generalizability.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Parents of 208 infants aged 4–12 months, recruited through users of the Nanit baby monitor, supplied up to two weeks of nightly computer-vision sleep data including total sleep time and parent visits to the crib, alongside questionnaires on infant temperament and parenting. Using dynamic structural equation modeling, the researchers separated night-to-night *variability* from *inertia* — how strongly one night predicts the next. Infants high in negative emotionality showed more inertia in sleep duration but less in parental visits; infants high in effortful control showed the reverse; and supportive parenting was associated with lower sleep-time inertia.
studies.why_it_matters: It shifts infant sleep research from "does this baby sleep well on average" to "how stuck is this baby in whatever pattern they're in" — and suggests a fussy baby's bad nights are more self-perpetuating, unless a responsive parent is in the loop.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the parent staring at an app graph at 4am trying to work out whether last night predicts tonight. The surprise is that the answer depends on the baby's temperament — and that supportive parenting appears to loosen the grip of a bad run of nights rather than simply adding hours. Call Lauren Bailes at Oklahoma State University. Avoid any implication that parents can be coached into a specific crib-visiting strategy; this is observational.
studies.wider_angle: For a technology or parenting outlet: consumer baby monitors with computer vision are quietly becoming a research instrument, generating nightly objective sleep data at a scale no sleep lab can match. What does it mean when developmental science runs on a subscription product's dataset — and whose babies end up in it?
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation. Sample recruited entirely from paying users of a commercial baby monitor, so skewed toward affluent households; temperament and parenting self-reported by the same parent; two-week observation window; the abstract's description of the design is internally inconsistent (states between-person methodology while reporting within-person models).

studies.title: It's how well you sleep, not how long, that tracks your heart and metabolic risk
studies.ns_score_reason: 25,000 adults and a clean quality-versus-duration contrast, but cross-sectional and self-reported throughout.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Analyzing 25,433 adults from the 2022 US National Health Interview Survey, researchers compared self-reported sleep duration and three sleep-quality measures against a count of four cardiometabolic risk factors: overweight/obesity, diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Poor sleep quality was associated with a 15–20% higher risk-factor burden, compared with 9% for short duration, and quality measures tracked more severe combinations of risk factors. The link between difficulty staying asleep and risk burden was significantly stronger in lower-socioeconomic-status groups.
studies.why_it_matters: Public messaging is almost entirely about hours; this suggests the fragmentation people experience — waking at 3am and not getting back — carries a stronger cardiometabolic signal, and that the same bad night may not mean the same thing for everyone.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the person who reliably logs seven and a half hours and still wakes at 3am every night — the sleep tracker says they're fine and this dataset suggests otherwise. Call Dayna Johnson at Emory, who has built a career on sleep and health equity, and ask about the SES interaction: why would waking in the night be worse for you if you're poorer? Keep it firmly observational — no claim that fixing sleep fixes blood pressure.
studies.wider_angle: A consumer-technology piece: wearables optimize for duration and "sleep score" composites because those are what accelerometers measure well, while the metric that looks more strongly associated with health here — difficulty staying asleep — is a subjective experience. Good fit for a tech or consumer-health outlet.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional — cannot establish causation or direction. All exposures and most outcomes self-reported. Single survey year. Risk-factor count treats very different conditions as equivalent units. Funded by NIH grants to the senior author.

studies.title: Parents who quit sleep training describe distress, exhaustion and disrupted breastfeeding
studies.journal: Journal of Reproductive and Infant Psychology
studies.ns_score_reason: fills a real gap on why behavioral sleep interventions have high dropout, but it is a ten-person qualitative study and reports experience, not outcome.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, researchers interviewed ten breastfeeding mothers in Australia who had started and then abandoned behavioral infant sleep interventions delivered in residential or inpatient settings. Five themes emerged: interventions that failed to adapt to individual families, loss of maternal agency on the ward, exhaustion and loss of pleasure in family life, perceived undermining of the breastfeeding relationship, and escalating distress across the family.
studies.why_it_matters: Behavioral sleep interventions are among the most-recommended and most-argued-about parenting tools, and dropout rates are high; this is the first structured account of what the people who leave actually experienced.
studies.pitch_angle: Open with a mother in a residential sleep unit being told to do something to her baby that she has decided she will not do. The hook is that the dropout statistics in sleep-training trials — usually a footnote about attrition — have content, and the content is about agency and breastfeeding, not about whether the technique "works." Call Andrew Lewis or Brittany Van Zanden at Federation University Australia. Frame carefully: this does not show the interventions are harmful, it shows how inflexible delivery lands.
studies.wider_angle: A reported feature for a general-interest or parenting outlet on the sleep-training culture war — the gulf between trial evidence (which is broadly reassuring about safety) and lived experience in clinical settings, and what "family-centered care" actually requires. Could be paired with the international variation in whether sleep training is recommended at all.
studies.caveats: Small N (10), qualitative and non-generalizable by design, recruited specifically among those who discontinued (so says nothing about those who completed), Australian inpatient/residential settings only, retrospective self-report, no outcome data.

studies.title: Switching on a CPAP machine calms blood pressure the same night — even in people without hypertension
studies.ns_score_reason: a large sample and a big effect size within a single night, but retrospective and dependent on an indirect blood-pressure measure.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In 464 adults who underwent split-night polysomnography between 2015 and 2023 — diagnosis in the first half of the night, positive airway pressure titration in the second — researchers used pulse transit time to derive beat-to-beat blood pressure and measured its overnight variability. Variability fell sharply once PAP started, by roughly 20 mmHg of standard deviation in both hypertensive and non-hypertensive patients, with large effect sizes (Cohen's d ≈ 0.9–1.0). The adjusted difference between the two groups was not significant.
studies.why_it_matters: The cardiovascular benefit of treating sleep apnea is usually framed as a slow accrual over months in people who already have high blood pressure; here the stabilization appears within hours and is just as large in people whose daytime readings are normal.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the immediacy — one half of one night. Open on a patient in a sleep lab at 1am as the mask goes on and the pressure trace flattens out. Call the sleep laboratory team at Health City Cayman Islands. The important nuance to protect: this is a within-night physiological change, not evidence about long-term cardiovascular outcomes, and split-night studies are not randomized.
studies.wider_angle: A technology-focused piece for a medical or engineering outlet on pulse transit time as a cuffless, continuous blood-pressure proxy — the same principle now appearing in consumer wearables, its validation problems, and what it would take to trust a wristband's overnight blood-pressure trace.
studies.caveats: Retrospective, single-center, no control group or randomization; blood pressure derived indirectly from pulse transit time rather than measured directly; first- and second-half-of-night comparison confounded by normal circadian and sleep-stage variation; no follow-up beyond the night itself.

studies.title: The people with the worst sleep in America sit at the intersection of several identities
studies.ns_score_reason: a quarter of a million people and a genuinely novel analytic method for quantifying intersecting inequities; the headline direction is not itself surprising.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Using 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data from 235,326 US adults, researchers applied Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy — a Bayesian method designed to estimate outcomes across intersecting social groups without the statistical fragility of running every subgroup separately. They divided the sample into 20 strata defined jointly by racialized identity and sex/sexual identity. Multiply marginalized groups, such as LGBQ+ people of color, had the highest prevalence of both short *and* long sleep duration.
studies.why_it_matters: Sleep inequity research usually examines race or sexuality one axis at a time; MAIHDA quantifies what happens where they overlap, and finds the burden concentrated at the intersections rather than added up along them.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the double finding — the same groups show up at both extremes of sleep duration, which is unusual and suggests something other than a simple "less sleep the more stress" story. Open on the mundane biology of a bad night and how unevenly it is distributed. Call Dougie Zubizarreta at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and ask why both tails, not just the short one.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-as-story piece for a statistics-curious or policy outlet: MAIHDA is spreading fast through epidemiology as a way to study intersectionality quantitatively. Explain how it works, what it fixes about conventional subgroup analysis, and where its critics say it overreaches.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational; sleep duration self-reported as a single item with no quality measure; trans and gender nonconforming people pooled into one stratum, likely masking heterogeneity; BRFSS is a telephone survey with known coverage and non-response biases; single survey year.

studies.title: Being aware you're dreaming is the easy part — controlling the dream is not
studies.ns_score_reason: intrinsically fascinating territory with a useful new conceptual distinction, but it is a narrative review with no new data.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: This narrative review takes apart an assumption baked into most lucid dreaming research and most of the commercial interest around it: that becoming lucid gives you control. The authors separate three things — lucidity, agency and control — and propose that dream control operates through both agentic (deliberate, goal-driven) and non-agentic (implicit, expectation-driven) routes. They survey what aspects of dreams can actually be influenced, which strategies people use, why individual differences are so large, and identify the absence of any standardized way to measure dream control.
studies.why_it_matters: Lucid dreaming is being pitched for nightmare therapy, skill rehearsal and creativity, and all of those applications depend on control rather than mere awareness — a distinction the field has mostly blurred.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the frustrated lucid dreamer who knows perfectly well they're dreaming and still cannot make themselves fly. The hook is the non-agentic route: the idea that what you expect to happen in a dream shapes it more reliably than what you decide to do. Call Cecilia Bonamino at Queensland University of Technology. Good peg for explaining why the therapeutic claims — especially for recurrent nightmares — are further from the finish line than the enthusiasm suggests.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a general-interest outlet on the lucid dreaming industry — wearable masks, audio cues, supplement stacks and app-based training — set against a literature that admits it has no standardized way to measure whether any of it produces control. Consumer-tech-meets-consciousness.
studies.caveats: Narrative review, not systematic; no new data; the agentic/non-agentic framework is proposed rather than tested; the underlying literature relies heavily on self-report from highly selected, unusually skilled dreamers.

studies.title: Honeybees nap in bursts all day, and their sleep may hold a lesson for AI
studies.ns_score_reason: the catastrophic-forgetting link is a genuinely fresh angle; held back by being invertebrate work in a review format.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: This review of invertebrate sleep is paired with new data from *Apis mellifera*: automated video analysis of antennal movement across day-long recordings, revealing polyphasic sleep patterns in honeybees. The authors set out what insect sleep shares with vertebrate sleep — immobility, raised arousal thresholds, homeostatic rebound, state-dependent neural activity — and where it diverges, then argue that these compact, tractable nervous systems are the right place to test hypotheses about sleep's role in memory consolidation and energy regulation. They extend this to computation, proposing insect sleep as inspiration for tackling catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks.
studies.why_it_matters: If a brain with under a million neurons still needs sleep to protect what it has learned, that constrains theories of what sleep is for — and offers a testable design principle for machine learning systems that overwrite old learning when trained on new tasks.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a bee, motionless, antennae drooping, being watched by a computer vision system for 24 hours straight. The hook is the connection between an insect's naps and one of the more stubborn failure modes in modern AI. Call Hong Lei at Arizona State University, and Maxim Bazhenov at UC San Diego, who works on exactly the sleep-and-catastrophic-forgetting link. Be clear this is animal work with a computational analogy, not a claim about human sleep.
studies.wider_angle: A machine learning feature for a technology or computing outlet: the small but growing group of researchers building explicit "sleep phases" into neural networks — offline replay, synaptic downscaling — and whether biological sleep is a genuine design template or a seductive metaphor.
studies.caveats: Animal-only work; primarily a review with limited new data; the AI connection is a proposal, not a demonstrated result; automated antennal-movement scoring is an indirect proxy for sleep state.

studies.title: A child's airway is most vulnerable between the ages of five and ten
studies.ns_score_reason: the challenge to a century-old growth curve is a nice hook, but it is a narrative review synthesizing existing imaging data.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: This narrative review synthesizes imaging and morphometric evidence on how the adenoids, palatine tonsils, lingual tonsils and tongue actually grow, and finds they don't follow Scammon's classical growth curves — the framework that has shaped thinking about lymphoid tissue since the 1930s. Adenoids peak at 6–8 years, earlier than predicted; palatine tonsils peak at 8–10; the front two-thirds of the tongue is near adult size by 8–10 while the back third keeps growing into adolescence. Because soft tissue and craniofacial bone mature on different schedules, the authors argue there is a transient "window of vulnerability" between roughly 5 and 10 years when soft tissue disproportionately narrows the airway.
studies.why_it_matters: Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea affects a meaningful slice of children and is frequently missed; a structure-specific timeline suggests when risk peaks and when orthodontic or surgical intervention has the best geometric rationale.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a snoring seven-year-old. The hook is that the classic textbook curve for how children's tissues grow turns out not to describe the throat at all, and the mismatch creates a predictable few-year window when the airway is at its tightest. Call Audrey Yoon, who holds appointments at Pacific's Dugoni School of Dentistry and Stanford's sleep medicine division. Avoid implying parents should seek intervention — this is a conceptual framework, not a screening protocol.
studies.wider_angle: A history-of-science piece for a medical or general-interest outlet on Scammon's growth curves — one of the most durable graphs in pediatrics, reproduced in textbooks for ninety years, now being unpicked structure by structure as imaging gets better.
studies.caveats: Narrative review, no new data, no systematic search reported; lingual tonsil developmental data acknowledged to be essentially absent in healthy children; the "window of vulnerability" is a conceptual synthesis, not an empirically derived risk period; authors are orthodontists proposing a framework for orthodontic assessment.

studies.title: AI can spot sleep apnea from an ECG — but it isn't detecting your airway
studies.ns_score_reason: the mechanistic reframing is the interesting bit; weakened by a small number of included studies and segment-level rather than patient-level accuracy.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A PRISMA-DTA-compliant diagnostic meta-analysis pooled 13 studies of AI models detecting obstructive sleep apnea from ECG-derived signals, finding pooled sensitivity of 0.88 and specificity of 0.89, with an AUC above 0.90. The more interesting finding is interpretive: performance stayed consistent across very different model architectures, which the authors argue means the models are latching onto stable physiological patterns rather than dataset quirks. Specifically, they conclude the algorithms are not detecting airway obstruction at all — they are reading downstream autonomic nervous system responses in the heart's rhythm.
studies.why_it_matters: Consumer wearables increasingly claim to flag sleep apnea, and this clarifies what such a signal actually represents — a cardiac shadow of a breathing event, not the breathing event itself, with implications for when the inference will break down.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the misdirection: your watch says "possible sleep apnea" and what it has really noticed is your autonomic nervous system flinching. Open on someone getting that notification. Call Ayşe Bulut at Yozgat Bozok University. The honest framing is that high segment-level accuracy is not the same as correctly diagnosing a person, and the piece should say so.
studies.wider_angle: A piece for a technology or medical-devices outlet on the interpretability turn in clinical AI — the shift from asking "how accurate is it?" to "what is it actually measuring?", using ECG-based apnea detection as the worked example alongside similar debates in dermatology and radiology AI.
studies.caveats: Only 13 studies included; moderate between-study heterogeneity; results are segment-level accuracy, which typically overstates patient-level diagnostic performance; the mechanistic interpretation is inference from consistency across architectures, not direct evidence; no patient-level data or external validation.

studies.title: A telehealth sleep program for children in foster care gets parents to stay the course
studies.ns_score_reason: first trauma-informed sleep intervention built for this population and near-perfect retention, but the trial reports only feasibility, not whether children slept better.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Forty-five foster and adoptive caregivers of children aged 2–5 were randomized to SAFE-T — a brief, trauma-informed behavioral sleep intervention delivered by telehealth — or to an education control. Twenty-one of 22 caregivers in the SAFE-T arm completed every session and the post-treatment assessment. Satisfaction was substantially higher in the intervention group (p = .005, Hedges' g = 0.92), and qualitative feedback on the content was broadly positive.
studies.why_it_matters: Children in foster care have high rates of sleep disturbance and their caregivers are among the hardest groups to retain in any intervention; showing that a trauma-informed program can be delivered remotely with almost no dropout clears a practical obstacle, though it doesn't yet show the sleep improves.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a three-year-old who has moved homes three times and cannot fall asleep in a bedroom that is safe. The hook is that standard behavioral sleep advice — extinction, controlled crying — sits awkwardly with a child whose distress at separation has a history behind it, and this is the first program built around that. Call Candice Alfano at Stony Brook University. Be explicit that this pilot measured whether families would do it, not whether it worked.
studies.wider_angle: A social-policy feature for a general-interest or public-affairs outlet: sleep as an under-recognized driver of placement breakdown in foster care. Exhausted caregivers are a documented reason placements fail, and almost no service commissioning treats children's sleep as an intervention point.
studies.caveats: Small N (45), pilot feasibility trial with no efficacy outcomes reported in the abstract, outcomes are caregiver-reported satisfaction and adherence, single center, 3-month follow-up, control condition was education only.

studies.title: An epilepsy treatment cleans up the EEG without necessarily helping the child
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean dissociation between a biomarker and the outcomes that matter, but a small, specialist, uncontrolled study.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Thirty-six children with epileptic encephalopathy featuring spike-wave activation in sleep received intravenous immunoglobulin, with spike-wave index measured from NREM sleep EEG at baseline, 6 and 12 months alongside seizure frequency, functional disability and behavioral scales. The spike-wave index fell substantially and durably, with large effect sizes. But changes in that index showed no significant association with changes in function or behavior, and the correlation with seizure outcome was weak and non-significant (ρ = −0.18, p = 0.29).
studies.why_it_matters: The spike-wave index is the defining measurement of this condition and is widely used to judge whether treatment is working; this suggests the number can improve markedly while the child's day-to-day functioning does not follow.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the gap between a reassuring trace on a screen and a child whose life hasn't changed. Open on a parent being told the EEG looks much better. Call Pınar Topaloğlu at Istanbul University, and ask what clinicians should do when the only objective measure they have turns out not to track the thing they care about. Note the study had no control arm, so improvements over 12 months cannot be attributed to the treatment.
studies.wider_angle: A broader piece for a medical or science-policy outlet on surrogate endpoints — the recurring pattern in which a measurable proxy is adopted because it is easy to quantify, then decouples from patient outcomes. Sits alongside similar stories in oncology, cardiology and Alzheimer's drug approval.
studies.caveats: Small N (36), no control group — so clinical improvement over 12 months cannot be attributed to IVIg; single center; functional and behavioral outcomes are caregiver-reported (PEDI, CBCL); prospective but uncontrolled; rare condition, so findings may not generalize.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- The long-sleep signal has now appeared twice in consecutive runs, from different outcomes and study designs. "Sleeping nine hours or more is linked to earlier death — sleeping six is not" (PMID 42744622) lands on the same asymmetry as last month's "It's long sleep, not short sleep, that tracks with inflammation in 30,000 US adults" (PMID 42546640): the biological and now mortality signal sits at the upper tail while short sleep washes out after adjustment. Both also intersect with the U-shaped "<6 or ≥9 hours" bracket used in "Heart-and-metabolic illness makes depression harder to recover from" (PMID 42628578).
- Quality beats duration, again. "It's how well you sleep, not how long, that tracks your heart and metabolic risk" (PMID 42648984) reproduces in 25,433 adults the central result of "Three nights of poor sleep predict next-day mood — and how long you slept doesn't" (PMID 42617377) — different outcome domain, same ordering of metrics.
- Sleep as a rationed resource keeps accumulating evidence. "The people with the worst sleep in America sit at the intersection of several identities" (PMID 42660768) and the socioeconomic interaction in PMID 42648984 sit directly alongside "'You can sleep when you die': how hustle culture rations sleep in women of colour" (PMID 42624738) and "Night and weekend shifts predict which toddlers get a bedtime routine" (PMID 42545383). The qualitative mechanism from August now has quantitative structure from September.

**Advances**
- PMID 42744622 advances PMID 42546640 on the single point that weakened it: with a median 30.8 years of follow-up, reverse causation from undiagnosed illness at baseline is much harder to invoke, and the paper offers a candidate mediator (systolic blood pressure) rather than leaving the long-sleep association unexplained.
- "Poor sleep and inactivity cluster together — and that pattern tracks bipolar disorder risk" (PMID 42723029) extends the composite-score critique that ran through last month's "Autistic children keep more regular bedtimes than their peers" (PMID 42593049): both show that collapsing behavior into one index hides separable patterns, but PMID 42723029 does it prospectively with latent profile analysis in 242,947 people.

**Counterpoints**
- "Night owls don't actually sleep worse than larks — their clocks are just shifted" (PMID 42751860) complicates the quality-over-duration story. Here an intrinsic trait widely assumed to degrade sleep quality produced a near-total null on quality measures and a clean difference only in phase — a reminder that "quality" is not a single thing either. It also echoes the earlier firefighter null in "Sleep quality doesn't predict firefighters' long-term resilience" (PMID 42495965).
- "How you use your phone predicts depression far better than how long you use it" (PMID 42759324) transplants the duration-versus-character argument out of sleep entirely — and notably finds sleep sitting awkwardly between the two patterns, neither cleanly a dose effect nor cleanly a problematic-use effect.

**New themes**
- Biomarker–outcome dissociation is new this run and did not feature in August: "An epilepsy treatment cleans up the EEG without necessarily helping the child" (PMID 42407303), "AI can spot sleep apnea from an ECG — but it isn't detecting your airway" (PMID 42747635) and "Switching on a CPAP machine calms blood pressure the same night" (PMID 42754769, using pulse transit time as a blood-pressure proxy).
- Infant and family sleep interventions arrive as a cluster: "Camera-tracked cribs reveal how a baby's temperament locks in their sleep pattern" (PMID 42470789), "Parents who quit sleep training describe distress, exhaustion and disrupted breastfeeding" (PMID 42725637) and "A telehealth sleep program for children in foster care gets parents to stay the course" (PMID 42725804). August had only adjacent material (PMID 42545383).
- Dream research shifts from clinical prevalence to mechanism: last month's "Half of people in a depressive episode also meet criteria for nightmare disorder" (PMID 42617369) is now joined by the conceptual unpicking of lucidity, agency and control in PMID 42728107 — relevant because imagery rehearsal for nightmares is exactly the application that assumes control follows awareness.
- Comparative and computational sleep is entirely new: "Honeybees nap in bursts all day, and their sleep may hold a lesson for AI" (PMID 42728400).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Almost nothing in sleep medicine is measured directly any more — the field runs on proxies, and this batch is unusually frank about the gap between the proxy and the thing. ECG-based AI detects apnea by reading the autonomic aftershock in heart rhythm rather than the airway itself (PMID 42747635); overnight blood pressure is inferred from pulse transit time rather than a cuff (PMID 42754769); the spike-wave index improves markedly under IVIg while children's function and behavior do not follow (PMID 42407303); actigraphy stands in for sleep in ultramarathoners whose low-level movement is exactly what actigraphy handles worst (PMID 42637627); nightly infant sleep now comes from computer vision in a commercial crib monitor (PMID 42470789); and self-reported quality outperforms self-reported duration for cardiometabolic risk (PMID 42648984) while chronotype turns out to differ in phase, not quality, once actigraphy is applied (PMID 42751860).

**Why pitch this now:** Consumer wearables are shipping apnea notifications and cuffless blood-pressure trends to hundreds of millions of wrists on exactly the inferential chains these papers are picking apart, and clinical sleep medicine is simultaneously discovering that its most-quantified endpoint can improve without the patient doing so.

**Angle:** A reported feature on what sleep instruments are actually detecting — the chain from a physiological event to a sensor signal to a clinical number to a decision — written through three worked examples (the ECG that never sees an airway, the EEG index that decoupled from the child, the crib camera that has become a research cohort), for readers who own a tracker or have been handed a sleep-study result and assume the number refers to what its name says.

**Potential headlines:**
- Sleep medicine's best numbers are measuring something else
- The apnea alert on your wrist is watching your heart, not your breathing
- When the brainwave trace improves and the child does not

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the "what is the sensor actually detecting" frame is concrete, reportable from these papers, and pairs naturally with the magazine's existing wearables coverage.
- **STAT** — the surrogate-endpoint half of the story (PMID 42407303) and the diagnostic-accuracy caveat that segment-level performance overstates patient-level diagnosis are squarely its territory.
- **MIT Technology Review** — the interpretability turn in clinical AI, with ECG apnea detection as an unusually clean case where the model's target and its signal are known to differ.
- **Undark** — for the harder edge: a commercial baby monitor's subscriber base functioning as a developmental cohort, and who ends up in the data.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Sleep — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-20 | **Studies reviewed:** 17
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind sleep digest (run 2026-09-20)

---

### Study 1: Sleeping nine hours or more is linked to earlier death — sleeping six is not
**PMID:** 42744622 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Effect estimate reported without its confidence interval, which is borderline** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Long sleepers had a 17% higher risk of death from any cause after adjustment"
- **Abstract says:** "long sleep duration was significantly associated with increased risks of all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio: 1.17, 95% confidence interval: 1.01, 1.35)"
- **Problem:** The point estimate is reported correctly, but the lower bound of the CI is 1.01 — the single positive finding in the paper only just clears significance. A digest that frames this as the counterweight to "the dominant public health message" should show the reader how fragile the estimate is, especially since the pitch angle leans hard on the asymmetry between long and short sleepers.
- **Suggested fix:** "Long sleepers had a 17% higher risk of death from any cause after adjustment (HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.01–1.35 — only just clearing significance); short sleepers showed no significant excess risk for all-cause or cardiovascular death."

**Issue B. Author first names not verifiable from the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call the Institute of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine team at National Taiwan University (Kuo-Liong Chien, Jiun-Yu Wang)"
- **Abstract says:** "Lin YC(1), Chien KL(1)(2)(3), Lin HJ(3)(4), Su TC(5), Wang J(1)(6)(7)"
- **Problem:** Initials match, and the institutional attribution is correct, but the expanded first names — particularly "Jiun-Yu Wang" for "Wang J" — cannot be confirmed from the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only. Worth a check before a writer cold-calls.
- **Suggested fix:** Verify both first names against the journal's author list before the pitch goes out.

**NS fit note:** 7/10 is defensible on design grounds (large prospective cohort, hard mortality outcome, 30.8-year median follow-up) but the exposure is a single self-reported questionnaire item at baseline and the headline association is borderline. I would score it 6.

---

### Study 2: How you use your phone predicts depression far better than how long you use it
**PMID:** 42759324 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline asserts a comparison the authors explicitly declined to test** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "How you use your phone predicts depression far better than how long you use it"
- **Abstract says:** "time spent using social networking sites was weakly associated with depression symptoms (r = 0.11), whereas problematic use showed a larger association (r = 0.29); no correlation ratio was calculated."
- **Problem:** Two things. "Predicts" implies prospective prediction from what is a synthesis of cross-sectional correlations. And the authors state outright that they did not compute a ratio between the two correlations — so "far better" is the digest's descriptive read of two numbers side by side, not a tested contrast. The caveats mention descriptive cross-domain comparisons generally, but not this specific non-test on the headline finding.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "How you use your phone tracks depression more closely than how long you use it". Body: add "the authors note no formal correlation ratio was calculated, so the gap between 0.11 and 0.29 is a descriptive contrast, not a tested difference."

**Issue B. NS fit score sits above what the evidence base supports** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — a prospectively registered umbrella review that directly tests the assumption behind screen-time limits; pulled down by the poor quality of the underlying reviews."
- **Abstract says:** "56 of 59 reviews were rated critically low by AMSTAR-2... ODAF is not a confirmed causal mechanism."
- **Problem:** The rationale text acknowledges the problem but the number doesn't move for it. Nearly the entire evidence base is rated critically low, the framework is explicitly hypothesis-generating, and publication-bias-restricted contrasts exist for only three of five domains. A 7 puts this on par with the 30-year mortality cohort.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10, with the same rationale text.

---

### Study 3: Night owls don't actually sleep worse than larks — their clocks are just shifted
**PMID:** 42751860 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Most" overstates the abstract's "several"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Across quantitative and qualitative sleep measures, and across most circadian and ultradian rhythm parameters, the two groups did not differ."
- **Abstract says:** "The results did not reveal significant differences in sleep features nor in several circadian or ultradian rhythmicity parameters."
- **Problem:** "Several" tells you some parameters showed no difference; "most" makes a quantitative claim about the proportion that the abstract does not support. The distinction matters because the whole hook rests on the breadth of the null.
- **Suggested fix:** "Across quantitative and qualitative sleep measures, and across several circadian and ultradian rhythm parameters, the two groups did not differ."

Everything else checks out: N = 84 (42/42), mean age 23.3, 64 females, one week of wrist actigraphy, significant differences in all circadian and ultradian phase indicators, steeper LIDS decline in morning types, and the first LIDS-based chronotype comparison. Caveats are appropriately scoped and the null is correctly hedged.

---

### Study 4: Poor sleep and inactivity cluster together — and that pattern tracks bipolar disorder risk
**PMID:** 42723029 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline implies the poor-sleep/low-activity profile is the high-risk group; the abstract puts it among the lower-risk ones** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Poor sleep and inactivity cluster together — and that pattern tracks bipolar disorder risk"
- **Abstract says:** "Using the Low LE8 score group as a reference, all four comparison profiles exhibited significant protective associations for both anxiety (Hazard Ratio [HR] range: 0.65-0.78, all p < 0.001) and bipolar disorder (HR range: 0.37-0.51, all p < 0.001)"
- **Problem:** The "Low physical activity with poor sleep" profile is one of the four comparison profiles, all of which had *lower* bipolar incidence than the Low LE8 score reference group. The abstract reports only HR ranges, not profile-specific estimates, so nothing in it singles out the sleep/inactivity cluster as carrying elevated risk. A reader will take "tracks bipolar disorder risk" to mean elevated risk in that group — the opposite of the direction relative to the reference. The digest body is accurate; the headline is not.
- **Suggested fix:** "Health behaviours cluster into five patterns — and lumping them into one score hides a poor-sleep, low-activity group" or "Five distinct health-behaviour profiles, and all four healthier ones track lower bipolar risk."

**Issue B. Novelty label doesn't fit the study type** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** New mechanism"
- **Abstract says:** "These results support person-centred, pattern-based approaches over composite scoring for neuropsychiatric risk stratification and hypothesis generation."
- **Problem:** This is an observational latent-profile risk-stratification study. No mechanism is proposed or tested; the authors frame it as hypothesis generation. The label sets an expectation the paper doesn't meet.
- **Suggested fix:** Change to "New method / analytic approach."

Sample size (242,947), median follow-up (13.8 years), case counts (11,419 anxiety, 341 bipolar, 40 schizophrenia), HR ranges, the exploratory-and-null schizophrenia framing and Gao's affiliation all check out.

---

### Study 5: Ultramarathon runners get 96 minutes of sleep during a 217km race — and hallucinate
**PMID:** 42637627 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. The 96-minute figure is not specific to the 217km route** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Ultramarathon runners get 96 minutes of sleep during a 217km race"
- **Abstract says:** "15 male athletes (45.1 ± 10.5 years), who participated in Brazil 135 Ultramarathon (135 km: n = 4; 217 km: n = 11)... Mean total sleep time during the race was 96.67 ± 88.71 minutes"
- **Problem:** 96.67 minutes is the mean across the whole sample, which mixed two race distances. Attaching it to the 217km route in the headline implies a distance-specific figure the abstract doesn't report. The SD (88.71) is also almost as large as the mean, i.e. enormous variation between runners.
- **Suggested fix:** "Ultramarathon runners average 96 minutes of sleep across a multi-day race — and some hallucinate."

**Issue B. A statistically uninformative null is presented as a substantive finding** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Crucially, how much a runner slept during the race was uncorrelated with finish time." / "sleeping less didn't make anyone faster, so the sleep that runners sacrifice on the assumption it's costing them time appears to buy nothing"
- **Abstract says:** "Mean total sleep time during the race... was not correlated with finish time (P = .81; r = 0.10; 95% CI -0.59 to 0.90)"
- **Problem:** The confidence interval spans -0.59 to 0.90 — essentially the entire possible range of a correlation, in a sample of 13. This null carries almost no information; it cannot support "sleeping less didn't make anyone faster" as a conclusion, and the pitch builds its "surprise" on it. The caveats flag small N but not that this specific finding is uninformative rather than negative.
- **Suggested fix:** "Sleep during the race showed no correlation with finish time, though with only 13 runners the estimate is far too imprecise to rule out an effect in either direction (r = 0.10, 95% CI -0.59 to 0.90)."

Sample (15 enrolled, 13 with sleep data), age, actigraphy windows, symptom counts (sleepiness n=5, balance n=4, hallucinations n=4), the pre-race sleep deprivation and the P = .058 trends are all accurate.

---

### Study 6: Moderate drinkers have enlarged choroid plexus — and it tracks their sleep problems
**PMID:** 42202661 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline says "moderate drinkers"; the exposure group was moderate-to-heavy** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Moderate drinkers have enlarged choroid plexus — and it tracks their sleep problems"
- **Abstract says:** "young adults who were moderate-to-heavy drinkers (HD) or light-to-non-drinkers (LD)"
- **Problem:** The comparison group is "moderate-to-heavy" versus "light-to-non", and the digest body itself switches to calling them "heavy drinkers" two sentences later. A headline reading "moderate drinkers" invites readers who drink modestly to place themselves in the affected group, when the group as defined includes heavy drinkers and is contrasted against people who drink very little or not at all.
- **Suggested fix:** "Moderate-to-heavy drinkers have enlarged choroid plexus — and it tracks their sleep problems"

Everything else verifies: N = 796 (399 HD / 397 LD), ages 22–37, HCP source, bilateral ChP enlargement with no total CSF difference, the within-HD correlations with sleep latency and sleep disturbance plus PSQI total in males, and the sex-split direction (HD females better on habitual sleep efficiency and duration, HD males worse on sleep latency). The digest correctly avoids the causal reading that the paper's own title ("predicts sleep disruption") invites.

---

### Study 7: Camera-tracked cribs reveal how a baby's temperament locks in their sleep pattern
**PMID:** 42470789 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. The framing of supportive parenting reverses the reported interaction** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "suggests a fussy baby's bad nights are more self-perpetuating, unless a responsive parent is in the loop" / "supportive parenting appears to loosen the grip of a bad run of nights"
- **Abstract says:** "When caregivers were higher in supportive parenting, there was a positive association between infant negative emotionality and TST inertia."
- **Problem:** The main effect (supportive parenting → lower TST inertia) is reported correctly in "The study". But the moderation goes the other way: at *higher* levels of supportive parenting, negative emotionality was *positively* associated with sleep-time inertia. So supportive parenting did not buffer the temperament–inertia link — if anything the link was stronger where parenting was more supportive. Both the "Why it matters" and the pitch angle build on the buffering reading.
- **Suggested fix:** "Why it matters: ...suggests a fussy baby's bad nights are more self-perpetuating — and, counterintuitively, that the temperament–inertia link was strongest in the most supportive households, a result the authors leave unexplained." Drop "unless a responsive parent is in the loop" and "loosen the grip" from the pitch.

**Issue B. "Locks in" implies causation in an observational design** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Camera-tracked cribs reveal how a baby's temperament locks in their sleep pattern"
- **Abstract says:** "infant negative emotionality was associated with more TST inertia and lower PVC inertia"
- **Problem:** "Locks in" reads as a causal mechanism. This is cross-sectional questionnaire data on temperament correlated with nightly sleep metrics; the pitch angle correctly says "this is observational," but the headline doesn't.
- **Suggested fix:** "Camera-tracked cribs show a baby's temperament tracks how stuck their sleep pattern gets"

N = 208, ages 4–12 months, Nanit recruitment, up to two weeks of nightly data, TST/PVC via computer vision, DSEM, and the three main directional findings all check out — as does the digest's sharp catch that the abstract says "between-person methodologies" while reporting within-person models.

---

### Study 8: It's how well you sleep, not how long, that tracks your heart and metabolic risk
**PMID:** 42648984 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline denies a duration association the study actually found** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It's how well you sleep, not how long, that tracks your heart and metabolic risk"
- **Abstract says:** "Population-average cardiometabolic risk factor count was 9% higher among short sleepers, 15% to 20% higher across poor sleep quality measures... Poor sleep quality and short sleep duration were associated with higher population-level cardiometabolic risk factor burden."
- **Problem:** The authors' own conclusion names both exposures. Short sleep was associated with a 9% higher risk-factor count; the finding is that quality shows a *stronger* association, not that duration shows none. The digest body reports this correctly, so it is the headline alone that overreaches — but it is the line that survives into a pitch email.
- **Suggested fix:** "How well you sleep tracks heart and metabolic risk more strongly than how long you sleep"

Sample (25,433), survey year, the four risk factors, the 15–20% vs 9% contrast, the more-severe-combinations finding and the SES interaction for difficulty staying asleep are all accurate. NIH funding correctly carried into caveats.

---

### Study 9: Parents who quit sleep training describe distress, exhaustion and disrupted breastfeeding
**PMID:** 42725637 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Parents" broadens a sample of breastfeeding mothers** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Parents who quit sleep training describe distress, exhaustion and disrupted breastfeeding"
- **Abstract says:** "explore the experiences of breastfeeding mothers (n = 10) who had discontinued behavioural sleep interventions"
- **Problem:** All ten participants were breastfeeding mothers. Given that one of the five themes is specifically about the breastfeeding relationship, generalizing to "parents" flattens the population in a way that matters for the story.
- **Suggested fix:** "Breastfeeding mothers who quit sleep training describe distress, exhaustion and a disrupted feeding relationship"

**Issue B. "First structured account" is not claimed in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this is the first structured account of what the people who leave actually experienced"
- **Abstract says:** "there is a lack of qualitative research exploring: a) the reasons why families disengage from these interventions, and b) how these interventions interact with the breastfeeding relationship."
- **Problem:** A gap in the literature is not the same as a first-of-its-kind claim. Unverifiable from abstract only, and priority claims are the kind of thing an editor will be asked to defend.
- **Suggested fix:** "this is a rare structured account of what the people who leave actually experienced."

The five themes, the IPA method, and the Australian residential/inpatient setting are reported accurately, and the caveats correctly note the sample is drawn only from those who discontinued. Author first names (Andrew Lewis, Brittany Van Zanden) are unverifiable from the abstract; note also that Van Zanden holds a second affiliation at University of Technology Sydney.

---

### Study 10: Switching on a CPAP machine calms blood pressure the same night — even in people without hypertension
**PMID:** 42754769 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline says CPAP and implies blood pressure fell; the study used PAP and measured variability** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Switching on a CPAP machine calms blood pressure the same night — even in people without hypertension"
- **Abstract says:** "positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy... NBPF was defined as the standard deviation of systolic blood pressure (SBP) derived from PTT"
- **Problem:** Two small slips. The intervention is PAP titration generally, not CPAP specifically. And "calms blood pressure" is likely to be read as blood pressure *falling*, when the outcome is the standard deviation of PTT-derived systolic pressure across the night — a variability measure. The body text handles both correctly.
- **Suggested fix:** "Starting airway pressure therapy steadies overnight blood pressure swings within hours — even in people without hypertension"

N = 464, split-night design, 2015–2023, reductions of 20.71 and 18.97 mmHg, Cohen's d of 0.96 and 0.90, and the non-significant adjusted between-group difference all verify. The digest deserves credit for declining to repeat the abstract's own clinical recommendation ("These findings support early PAP initiation"), and for flagging the first-half/second-half circadian confound the authors don't mention.

---

### Study 11: The people with the worst sleep in America sit at the intersection of several identities
**PMID:** 42660768 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Caveat mischaracterizes how trans and gender nonconforming people were handled** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "trans and gender nonconforming people pooled into one stratum, likely masking heterogeneity"
- **Abstract says:** "grouping participants into 20 intersectional social strata... jointly defined by racialized identity (Black, Latine, White, multiracial/other) and sex/sexual identity (heterosexual-cisgender males, heterosexual-cisgender females, LGBQ-cisgender males, LGBQ-cisgender females, trans and gender nonconforming people)"
- **Problem:** Four racialized categories × five sex/sexual identity categories = the 20 strata, so TGNC people were crossed with racialized identity and appear across four strata, not one. The real limitation is that TGNC people were collapsed into a single sex/sexual identity category rather than disaggregated by gender identity or sexual orientation — a defensible caveat, just not the one written.
- **Suggested fix:** "trans and gender nonconforming people collapsed into a single sex/sexual identity category rather than disaggregated, likely masking heterogeneity"

N = 235,326, BRFSS 2022, the MAIHDA description, the 20 strata and the both-tails finding for multiply marginalized groups are accurate, and the digest correctly resists turning the authors' policy conclusion into a recommendation.

---

### Study 12: Being aware you're dreaming is the easy part — controlling the dream is not
**PMID:** 42728107 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Pitch hook asserts a comparative claim the review does not make** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The hook is the non-agentic route: the idea that what you expect to happen in a dream shapes it more reliably than what you decide to do."
- **Abstract says:** "we propose that dream control can occur through both agentic (deliberate, goal-driven) and non-agentic (implicit, expectation-driven) forms."
- **Problem:** The review proposes two coexisting routes. It makes no claim that the expectation-driven route is *more reliable* than the deliberate one — and since the authors also identify the lack of any standardized way to measure dream control, no such comparison could be supported. The hook the writer would pitch on is not in the paper.
- **Suggested fix:** "The hook is the non-agentic route: the proposal that what you implicitly expect to happen in a dream shapes it alongside — and sometimes despite — what you deliberately try to do."

The narrative-review status, the lucidity/agency/control distinction, the survey of influenceable dream aspects and individual differences, the standardized-measurement gap, and Bonamino's QUT affiliation all check out, and the caveats are appropriately blunt about the framework being proposed rather than tested.

---

### Study 13: Honeybees nap in bursts all day, and their sleep may hold a lesson for AI
**PMID:** 42728400 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Neuron count is not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "If a brain with under a million neurons still needs sleep to protect what it has learned, that constrains theories of what sleep is for"
- **Abstract says:** "Insects combine compact nervous systems with well-characterized learning behaviors"
- **Problem:** The figure is a commonly cited estimate for *Apis mellifera*, but it is not in this abstract — unverifiable from abstract only. The second half of the sentence also asserts that the bee brain "needs sleep to protect what it has learned," whereas the abstract only says the comparison "inform[s] hypotheses about sleep's adaptive roles in memory consolidation." The conditional "if" softens it, but a reader will take the premise as established.
- **Suggested fix:** "If a brain as compact as a bee's still needs sleep — and the authors treat memory consolidation as a hypothesis, not a settled role — that constrains theories of what sleep is for"

The review-plus-new-data structure, the automated video analysis of antennal movement over day-long recordings, the polyphasic finding in *Apis mellifera*, the list of shared vertebrate/invertebrate features, the catastrophic-forgetting proposal and both named contacts (Lei at ASU, Bazhenov at UC San Diego) verify. The caveats correctly label the AI link a proposal.

---

### Study 14: A child's airway is most vulnerable between the ages of five and ten
**PMID:** 42762282 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline states a conceptual window as an established fact** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A child's airway is most vulnerable between the ages of five and ten"
- **Abstract says:** "creating a transient 'window of vulnerability' between approximately 5 and 10 years of age" — in a "narrative review" offering "a conceptual, site-specific clinical framework"
- **Problem:** The authors put "window of vulnerability" in scare quotes, prefix it with "approximately," and label the whole framework conceptual. The digest's own caveats say exactly this, but the headline reads as an empirical finding about children's airways. For a paediatric-airway claim that parents might act on, the gap between headline and caveat is worth closing.
- **Suggested fix:** "Children's airways may be most vulnerable between five and ten, a new framework argues"

**Issue B. Two contextual claims not sourced to the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea affects a meaningful slice of children and is frequently missed" / "the framework that has shaped thinking about lymphoid tissue since the 1930s"
- **Abstract says:** "Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is closely linked to the growth and interaction of upper airway soft tissues" and refers to Scammon's curves having "long provided a fundamental framework" without dating them.
- **Problem:** Prevalence, underdiagnosis and the 1930s date are all plausible and probably correct from the wider literature, but none is verifiable from this abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only — source them independently before the pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** Attribute both to external sources, or cut the underdiagnosis clause.

The structure-specific peaks (adenoids 6–8, palatine tonsils 8–10, anterior tongue near adult size by 8–10, posterior third into adolescence), the absence of lingual tonsil normative data, and Yoon's dual Pacific/Stanford affiliation all check out, as does the caveat noting the authors' orthodontic framing.

### Study 15: AI can spot sleep apnea from an ECG — but it isn't detecting your airway
**PMID:** 42747635 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. The authors' double-hedged inference is restated as a firm conclusion** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Specifically, they conclude the algorithms are not detecting airway obstruction at all — they are reading downstream autonomic nervous system responses in the heart's rhythm." (and headline: "but it isn't detecting your airway")
- **Abstract says:** "these findings suggest that AI systems may not directly detect airway obstruction but instead may identify downstream physiological responses, particularly autonomic nervous system alterations reflected in cardiovascular signals."
- **Problem:** "Suggest... may not directly... may identify" becomes "conclude... not at all... they are reading." Three layers of hedging removed, and "not directly" is turned into "not at all," which is a stronger claim. This matters because the mechanistic reframing is the whole reason the entry is in the digest, and the caveats correctly note it is an inference from architectural consistency rather than direct evidence — the body text contradicts that caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "Specifically, they suggest the algorithms may not be detecting airway obstruction directly — they may instead be reading downstream autonomic nervous system responses in the heart's rhythm." Headline: "AI can spot sleep apnea from an ECG — but it may not be detecting your airway."

Thirteen included studies, pooled sensitivity 0.88 and specificity 0.89, AUC above 0.90, moderate heterogeneity, the consistency-across-architectures observation, the PRISMA-DTA compliance, segment-level framing and Bulut's affiliation all verify. The caveat that segment-level accuracy overstates patient-level performance is a good catch.

### Study 16: A telehealth sleep program for children in foster care gets parents to stay the course
**PMID:** 42725804 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. N = 45 randomized (22 SAFE-T / 23 control), children aged 2–5, telehealth delivery, 21/22 completing all sessions and the post-treatment assessment, satisfaction p = .005 with Hedges' g = 0.92, favourable qualitative feedback, 3-month follow-up and Alfano's Stony Brook affiliation all check out. The digest is explicit in three separate places that this is feasibility and acceptability only — "it doesn't yet show the sleep improves," "measured whether families would do it, not whether it worked" — which is exactly the right handling of a pilot RCT, and the NS fit of 4/10 reflects that honestly. ("Single center" is unverifiable from the abstract but is a conservative caveat rather than a claim.)

### Study 17: An epilepsy treatment cleans up the EEG without necessarily helping the child
**PMID:** 42407303 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. The digest states that clinical outcomes did not improve; the abstract reports that they did** — Severity: Major

- **As written:** "An epilepsy treatment cleans up the EEG without necessarily helping the child" / "this suggests the number can improve markedly while the child's day-to-day functioning does not follow" / "Open on a parent being told the EEG looks much better" against "a child whose life hasn't changed"
- **Abstract says:** "Seizure frequency decreased and clinical scale scores improved during follow-up." And: "IVIg therapy was associated with significant and sustained electrophysiological improvement and is accompanied by clinical improvement in children with EE-SWAS and DEE-SWAS. However, changes in SWI were not significantly correlated with functional, behavioral, or seizure outcomes"
- **Problem:** This reverses the clinical finding. Seizure frequency fell and clinical scale scores improved over follow-up. What the study found is a *dissociation between the magnitude of EEG change and the magnitude of clinical change* — SWI reduction did not predict who improved functionally or behaviourally. That is a genuine and interesting surrogate-endpoint story, and the digest's "wider angle" frames it correctly. But the headline, the "Why it matters" and the pitch's opening image all tell readers the children did not improve, which is factually wrong and could mislead a writer into calling a clinician with a false premise. (The uncontrolled design means the improvement can't be attributed to IVIg — a point the caveats make correctly — but "can't be attributed to the drug" is a different claim from "didn't happen.")
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "The EEG marker used to judge this epilepsy treatment doesn't track how the child actually does." Why it matters: "The spike-wave index is the defining measurement of this condition and is widely used to judge whether treatment is working; here both the index and the children's clinical scores improved over 12 months, but the size of the EEG change bore no relationship to the size of the clinical change — so the number cannot stand in for the outcome." Pitch: open on a parent told the EEG looks much better, and the clinician who cannot say what that means for this particular child.

N = 36, prospective enrolment, SWI from NREM sleep EEG at baseline/6/12 months, the large effect sizes, the null multivariable associations with PEDI and CBCL change, and ρ = −0.18, p = 0.29 for seizure outcome are all reported accurately, and the no-control-arm limitation is correctly flagged in both the pitch and the caveats.

**Cross-cutting note for the editor:** twelve of the seventeen issues sit in headlines or pitch hooks rather than in the "The study" paragraphs, which are generally well checked. The recurring pattern is a body text that hedges properly and a headline that drops the hedge — studies 4, 8, 14, 15 and 17 all follow it. Worth a single pass over headlines alone before anything goes to pitch.
